notes.12:49: Literally "what do I wish if it has already been kindled?", a Semitic idiom expressing intense desire.
notes.12:59: Greek lepton, the smallest bronze coin circulating in Judea, worth one-eighth of an assarion (compare 12:6).
notes.13:4: "Offenders" translates Greek opheiletai (literally "debtors"), a Semitic idiom denoting moral guilt before God.
notes.13:9: The Greek clause breaks off abruptly after "in the time to come" (aposiopesis), leaving an implied positive outcome such as "well and good."
notes.13:21: "Three measures" renders Greek sata tria (three Hebrew seahs), a large volume of roughly 35 to 40 liters of flour.
notes.13:32: Greek teleioumai can mean "I reach completion" (finishing His appointed course) or "I am brought to perfection" through suffering.
notes.13:35: The Greek text reads simply "your house is left to you," without the word "desolate" found in some later manuscripts and Matthew 23:38.
notes.14:2: "Dropsy" translates Greek hydropikos, a condition characterized by abnormal fluid retention and swelling in the body (edema).
notes.14:5: The Greek text reads "a son or an ox" (huios e bous), strongly attested in early witnesses; other manuscripts read "a donkey or an ox" (onos e bous).
notes.14:18: "All alike" renders the elliptical Greek idiom apo mias (literally "from one [mind/voice]"), meaning unanimously or one and all.
notes.14:24: "You" is plural (hymin), shifting from the single slave addressed in v. 23 so that the host's final declaration also speaks directly to Jesus' listeners.
notes.14:26: In Semitic idiom, "hate" (miseo) is used hyperbolically for loving less or subordinating all other allegiances to devotion to Jesus (cf. Matthew 10:37).
notes.15:7: The Greek omits an explicit comparative ("more"), using a Semitic idiom in which "joy ... than" carries the sense "more joy ... than."
notes.15:8: A drachma was a Greek silver coin roughly equivalent to a Roman denarius, about a day's wage for a common laborer.
notes.15:21: Some ancient manuscripts add "make me like one of your hired workers" at the end of the verse, likely assimilated from verse 19; the shorter text is better attested.
notes.16:6: A "bath" was a Hebrew liquid measure of about 8 to 9 gallons (30 to 35 liters); in verse 7, a "kor" was a dry measure of about 10 to 11 bushels (350 to 400 liters).
notes.16:8: Greek ho kyrios ("the master" or "the Lord") refers here to the rich master of the parable rather than Jesus, as confirmed by the shift to Jesus's own voice in verse 9 ("And I tell you").
notes.16:9: "Unrighteous wealth" renders the literal Semitic expression "the mammon of unrighteousness" (from Aramaic mamona, referring to wealth or material possessions).
notes.16:16: The verb biazetai is debated: taken as middle voice it means "forces his way into it," while taken as passive it can mean "is strongly urged into it."
notes.16:22: Literally "into Abraham's bosom," an idiom expressing the place of honor reclining next to a host at a banquet.
notes.17:10: "Unworthy" translates Greek achreioi, which literally means "useless" or "unprofitable," referring here to slaves who have earned no special merit beyond their required duty.
notes.17:11: The Greek phrase dia meson Samareias kai Galilaias can be understood either as "between Samaria and Galilee" (along their border) or "through the middle of Samaria and Galilee."
notes.17:21: The Greek phrase entos hymon is debated and can mean either "in your midst" (among you) or "within you."
notes.17:35: Verse 36 ("Two men will be in the field; one will be taken and the other will be left") is absent from the earliest and best Greek manuscripts and is omitted in the critical text.
notes.17:37: The Greek word aetoi can mean either "vultures" or "eagles"; "vultures" fits the proverb's imagery of carrion birds gathering around a body (soma).
notes.18:5: The Greek verb hypopiazo literally means "to strike under the eye" and is used figuratively here for wearing someone down or exhausting them; eis telos can mean either "continually" or "finally."
notes.18:7: The clause kai makrothymei ep' autois is syntactically debated: makrothymeo can mean "is patient over them" as an accompanying remark or "delays long over them" as a continuation of the rhetorical question.
notes.18:11: The phrase pros heauton ("to himself") stands directly before proseucheto ("was praying") in this text, suggesting silent or self-directed prayer, though some link it with statheis ("standing by himself").
notes.18:42: The Greek verb sesoken literally means "has saved" (matching 18:26) and in Luke's healing narratives carries the dual sense of physical healing ("made well") and spiritual salvation.
notes.19:8: The Greek present-tense verbs "I give" (didōmi) and "I pay back" (apodidōmi) are debated as either a resolve taking immediate effect or a statement of Zacchaeus's ongoing practice; keeping the simple present preserves both possibilities.
notes.19:13: A mina (mna) was a unit of silver currency equal to 100 drachmas, roughly three to four months' wages for an ordinary laborer.
notes.19:42: The opening clause is an unfinished conditional sentence (aposiopesis) expressing deep grief and an unfulfilled wish, literally "If you had known on this day, even you, the things toward peace—".
notes.19:46: The Greek text here omits the future verb "will be" (estai) found in some manuscripts (cf. Isa 56:7), reading a verbless clause literally "My house [is] a house of prayer."
notes.20:18: "Crush to powder" translates the Greek verb likmao, which originally means "winnow" and is used here (as in LXX Daniel 2:44) in the sense of pulverizing or scattering like dust.
notes.20:21: "Show partiality" renders the Semitic idiom lambano prosopon (literally, "receive a face"), meaning to favor someone based on outward appearance or status.
notes.20:30: The earliest manuscripts contain only "and the second," linking directly to v. 31; later manuscripts expand the verse to state that he took the wife and died childless.
notes.20:36: "Equal to angels" renders the rare Greek compound isangelos, occurring only here in the New Testament, pointing specifically to immortality in the resurrection.
notes.20:37: "In the passage about the bush" renders epi tes batou (literally, "at the bush"), an ancient convention for citing a Scripture section—here the burning-bush account in Exodus 3.
notes.21:2: A lepton (plural lepta) was the smallest bronze coin in circulation in first-century Judea, worth a tiny fraction of a day's wage.
notes.21:19: The critical text reads the aorist imperative ("gain"), whereas some manuscripts read the future indicative ("you will gain"). Greek psychas can denote either "souls" or "lives."
notes.21:25: The critical text reads the genitive noun "roaring" (echous), whereas later manuscripts read the participle "roaring" (echouses) modifying "sea."
notes.21:36: The critical text reads "have strength" (katischysete), whereas some later manuscripts read "be counted worthy" (kataxiothete).
notes.22:15: "With longing I have longed" literally reflects the Greek cognate-dative idiom (epithymia epethymesa), a Semitic construction expressing intense desire.
notes.22:19: The words from "which is being given for you" through the end of verse 20 are omitted in Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses, but are strongly supported by the earliest Greek manuscripts, including P75, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus.
notes.22:31: In Greek, "you" in verse 31 (hymas) is plural, encompassing all the disciples, whereas "you" in verse 32 (sou, sy) shifts to the singular, addressing Simon Peter individually.
notes.22:36: "The one who has none" (ho me echon) has no stated object in Greek; it may refer either to lacking a moneybag and knapsack or, anticipating the end of the clause, to lacking a sword.
notes.22:43: Verses 43–44 are omitted by several early manuscripts (including P75, Vaticanus, and Alexandrinus), while attested by Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae, early patristic writers, and the majority of later witnesses.
notes.22:51: "Leave it at this!" (eate heos toutou) is variously understood either as stopping the disciples ("No more of this!") or as addressing the arresting group ("Permit even this," so He might heal the slave's ear).
notes.22:70: "You yourselves say that I am" (hymeis legete hoti ego eimi) is a reserved yet affirmative idiom in Greek, acknowledging the claim while leaving the phrasing to the questioners.
notes.23:18: Verse 17 (mentioning an obligation to release one prisoner at the festival) is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts and from the Saints Greek Critical Text, which moves directly from 23:16 to 23:18.
notes.23:34: Jesus' prayer for forgiveness ("Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing") is absent from several early manuscripts (including P75, B, and D*) but is well attested in other early witnesses and patristic citations, and stands in this Greek text.
notes.23:43: The Greek text has no punctuation around "today" (semeron); placing the comma before "today" matches Luke's regular idiom after "Truly I say to you" rather than attaching "today" to "I say."
notes.23:45: The phrase tou heliou eklipontos literally means "as the sun failed" (a verb often used of an eclipse, though a Passover full moon rules out a natural solar eclipse); many later manuscripts read "and the sun was darkened."
notes.23:54: The verb epephosken literally means "was dawning" or "was growing light," used here for the approach of the Jewish Sabbath day beginning at sunset.
notes.24:12: This verse is absent from Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses (a Western non-interpolation), though strongly attested in P75, Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus. Following the Greek punctuation, the idiom 'πρὸς ἑαυτόν' modifies 'went away' ('to his home'), though it can also be construed with 'marveling' ('marveling to himself').
notes.24:13: Sixty stadia is approximately seven miles (about eleven kilometers); a few later witnesses read 'one hundred sixty stadia'.
notes.24:47: The participle 'beginning' (ἀρξάμενοι) is nominative masculine plural, linking grammatically with 'you' in verse 48 rather than with the accusative 'repentance'.
notes.24:51: The clause 'and was carried up into heaven' (along with 'after worshiping Him' in verse 52) is absent from a few early witnesses such as original Sinaiticus and Codex Bezae, but is widely supported by P75, Vaticanus, and the majority of manuscripts.
